transcript: Last night, I saw Real Women Have Curves on Broadway. This is a new musical set in 1987 Los Angeles following a group of women working at a garment factory owned and operated by the family of our protagonist Ana García. While Ana's older sister Estela who manages the factory is focused on impressing a major new client to bring the family business to new heights, Ana has some dreams of her own. She wants to go to college and move to New York to become a writer, but she's struggling to reconcile her dreams with the responsibilities she has at home, which are heightened by the fact that Ana is the only US citizen in her family. Of course, the Latin American representation and the body diversity that the show brings to Broadway is worth celebrating. But also, this is just a great musical because it nails the fundamentals of theatrical storytelling. The character relationships are believable, the story has a strong emotional core, and there are clear dramatic stakes for every character. Despite some of the more serious topics involved in the plot, like the immigrant experience, this show avoids the common trap of becoming weighed down by its themes. It's a musical comedy through and through. The Latin-infused score and charming script, coupled with snappy pacing and solid performances across the board, makes this one of the few truly feel-good musicals of the season. With that, another playbill for my collection.
